title: Leaked: HYBE, SM, JYP, YG's Secret Seoul Summit Reveals a $30B Japan Streaming Gambit
excerpt: Over 50 K-pop entertainment companies — including all Big 4 agencies — gathered in Seoul to craft a unified Japan streaming market strategy. With 1.42 billion new plays and a paradigm shift from intuition to data, here's what their blueprint looks like.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
On February 6, 2026, something unprecedented happened in the heart of Seoul.

HYBE, SM Entertainment, JYP Entertainment, YG Entertainment — the so-called Big 4 — along with **over 50 entertainment companies** sat down at the same table. In an industry defined by cutthroat competition, rivals rarely share a room, let alone a strategy session. But on that day, they all came for one reason: **Japan**.

At the 2026 Korea Music Data Summit, a single number changed the atmosphere in the room. Japan's premium music streaming plays surged by **1.42 billion year-over-year**. That number alone was enough to make every executive in attendance recalculate their priorities.

## 1.42 Billion Plays — Why This Number Is a Game-Changer

To put 1.42 billion in perspective: that increase alone **rivals the combined annual paid streaming volume of Taiwan and Thailand**. Japan's dominance in the Asia-Pacific paid audio streaming market isn't just a lead — it's a chasm.

This matters even more when you consider what's happening at home. K-pop physical album sales in South Korea **plunged 19% in 2024**, dropping to 93.3 million units from 115.7 million in 2023 — the first decline after nine consecutive years of growth. Through November 2025, sales continued to slide, down another 2.56 million units year-over-year.

While Korea's domestic market hits a ceiling, Japan is moving in the exact opposite direction.

## 'Intuition Is Dead' — Data Takes the Wheel

The summit's most powerful declaration was unmistakable:

> **"Intuition-driven approaches to the Japanese market are no longer viable."**

Speakers urged Korean artists and labels to pivot to data-driven analysis — tracking local consumption patterns, fanbase behavior, and monetization models with surgical precision.

Specifically, Japanese streaming data should now dictate **release timing, platform prioritization, and tour planning**. The summit highlighted that converting fan engagement into revenue models is particularly effective in the Japanese market.

This represents a fundamental break from how K-pop agencies have traditionally approached Japan. The old playbook — "release a Japanese-language version + hold fan meetings" — worked in the CD era. But streaming has fundamentally reshaped Japanese consumer behavior, and the old formula simply doesn't cut it anymore.

![K-pop agencies unite for Japan streaming market strategy — the dawn of data-driven expansion](/images/news/kpop-big4-japan-streaming-strategy-body.webp)
_Over 50 K-pop entertainment companies gathered in Seoul to develop a data-driven strategy for Japan's booming streaming market_

## Big 4's Japan Playbooks — Different Paths, Same Destination

What's fascinating is how each of the Big 4 is approaching Japan with a distinct strategy.

**HYBE** is the most aggressive. With BTS already holding near-national-idol status in Japan, SEVENTEEN, ENHYPEN, and TXT are relay-touring Japanese domes to expand the empire. BTS's "Arirang" world tour Tokyo dates in April 2026 are expected to push HYBE's Japan revenue to record heights.

**SM Entertainment** is Japan's original K-pop powerhouse. Building on TVXQ's 20-year foundation, newer acts like aespa and RIIZE are scaling up their Japanese activities. RIIZE's upcoming Japanese studio album sits at the core of SM's streaming-first Japan strategy.

**JYP** wields a unique weapon: MISAMO (TWICE's Japanese-member unit) alongside Stray Kids. Operating a sub-unit composed of TWICE's Japanese members is a localization model no other agency has replicated.

**YG** is re-entering the Japan market behind BLACKPINK's return. Promotion for their February mini-album "Deadline" has already kicked into high gear in Japan.

## Why Japan, Why Now

Japan didn't suddenly become important — it has always been the world's second-largest music market. But the current all-in push from K-pop has structural reasons behind it.

**First, the paid streaming conversion is accelerating.** Japan has long been a CD-centric market. But paid streaming subscribers are now growing explosively. For K-pop agencies, this opens a new revenue pipeline — digital income without CD pressing costs, logistics, or physical distribution overhead.

**Second, purchasing power.** Japanese music consumers spend more per capita than anywhere else in the Asia-Pacific. Beyond paid streaming subscriptions, the percentage of fans who open their wallets for merchandise, fan club memberships, and concert tickets is overwhelmingly high.

**Third, the domestic ceiling.** With Korean album sales declining and fandom fatigue setting in, growth must come from overseas. K-pop album exports hit a record **$301.7 million** in 2025, but domestic sales keep shrinking. To bridge this gap, agencies need to lock down the biggest market closest to home — and that's Japan.

## What This Summit Means for K-Pop's Future

This wasn't just another industry event. It's a signal that K-pop is shifting its strategic axis from **"breadth of expansion" to "depth of penetration."**

Until now, K-pop's global strategy has been about reaching as many markets as possible: 12-city world tours, simultaneous releases in 15 countries, global fan voting. The focus was on spreading wide. But 50 companies simultaneously agreeing to "go deep on Japan" marks a fundamental recognition that depth creates more value than breadth.

The emphasis on **data-driven decision-making** is particularly significant. When agencies that once ran on instinct and gut feeling start building strategies around streaming data, fan behavior analytics, and monetization metrics, it marks K-pop's evolution from a "cultural industry" into a "data industry."

## Final Thoughts

On February 6, 2026, rivals in Seoul's most competitive industry set down their swords — just for a moment. And they all looked in the same direction. East.

A consensus forged by 1.42 billion plays. A sense of urgency born from a shrinking domestic market. And the recognition that the world's second-largest music market is undergoing a digital transformation that represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

The era of intuition is over. The era of data has begun. And on the Japanese battlefield, the Big 4's real war is just getting started.
